name: Wireframing
description:
Wireframing represents the structure and organisation of a digital interface without requiring finished visual styling. Wireframes typically show content hierarchy, controls, navigation and relationships between interface elements.

Their reduced visual detail allows designers to examine structure and interaction before typography, imagery and visual identity dominate discussion.
whenToUse: Use wireframes when moving from flows and requirements toward interface layouts and when the main questions concern hierarchy, navigation and interaction rather than final appearance.
steps: Define the user goal and relevant content.
Review the task or user flow.
Identify the elements required on each screen or state.
Arrange those elements according to hierarchy and task priority.
Connect screens to represent important interactions.
Create alternative layouts for uncertain areas.
Review the wireframes against scenarios and accessibility requirements.
Increase visual fidelity only when structural questions have been addressed.
lookOutFor: Wireframes can prematurely lock teams into familiar screen layouts.
Placeholder content can hide genuine content-design problems; use realistic content where possible.
Low visual fidelity does not remove the need to consider accessibility, responsive behaviour and information hierarchy.

resources.citation: Garrett, J. J. (2011). *The Elements of User Experience*, 2nd ed. New Riders.
Buxton, B. (2007). *Sketching User Experiences*. Morgan Kaufmann.
